## Methods

Human participants
Patients attending the McMaster University Celiac Clinic were recruited after signing informed consent. New cases of CeD (consuming gluten) were diagnosed based on positive serological markers, the presence of either HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8, and evaluation of duodenal biopsies (n=16). Treated CeD (T-CeD) included patients with a verified diagnosis, who were on GFD >2 years and attending the clinic as part of their follow-up (n=11). Healthy controls included patients attending the McMaster University Digestive Diseases Clinic with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease without other symptoms, and/or having confirmed normal endoscopy and biopsy, negative celiac serology, and negative Helicobacter pylori. They also did not fulfill the criteria for disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI) based on Rome IV criteria58. All participants were asked to complete a validated food frequency questionnaire (Victoria Cancer Council Dietary Questionnaire for Epidemiological Studies v2) to assess their habitual diet, and a validated gastrointestinal symptoms ratings score (GSRS)59,60 to assess symptoms. No participant had prescribed proton pump inhibitors, antibiotics, probiotics, or fiber supplementation at the time of sample collection. Sex, but not gender information, was collected and included in the analysis. The study was registered at clinicaltrials.gov (ID: NCT06532110) and approved by the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board (HiREB #15311). For details, see Supplementary Data 1.

Human sample collection
Fecal samples were collected and stored in anaerobic packages. After transport to the hospital, the samples were aliquoted in an anaerobic chamber (90% CO2, 5% H2, 5% N2)61. Duodenal aspirates were collected during endoscopy, mixed with 10% glycerol and aliquoted in aerobic conditions62. All samples were frozen at −80 °C until analysis.

Mouse model
Breeding pairs of non-obese diabetic AB°DQ8 (NOD/DQ8) mice63 were originally received from Dr. Joseph Murray (Mayo Clinic, USA)43. Female and male specific-pathogen-free (SPF) mice were bred and housed in the McMaster Central Animal Facility (CAF) and were 8–10 weeks old and sex-matched for all experimental groups. SPF mice were housed in clean rooms, with ad libitum water and an irradiated grain-based diet formulated without gluten (GFD, TD.05620, Envigo; Table 2). The rooms had a 12-h dark/light cycle, and at room temperature and ambient humidity was maintained between 40–60%. Germ-free (GF) NOD/DQ8 mice were generated by two-stage embryo transfer and housed within the McMaster Axenic Gnotobiotic Unit (AGU) in flexible film isolators with free access to autoclaved food and water44. Diets were autoclaved to ensure sterility. Mice were sacrificed under anaesthesia (Isofluorane) using cervical dislocation before necropsy and tissue collection. All experiments were conducted with approval from the McMaster University Animal Care Committee and McMaster Animal Research Ethics Board (AREB) under the Animal Utilization Protocol (AUP #210930).

Gluten sensitization and dietary interventions
To minimize litter and cage effects, littermates were distributed across treatment groups using random assignment to sex-balanced cages before sensitization with gluten using an established protocol where mice were gavaged with 25 μg cholera toxin and 1 mg of pepsin/trypsin-digested gliadin once a week for 3 weeks23. Mice were then switched from a gluten-free diet (TD.05620) to a calorically balanced gluten-containing wheat-based diet (TD.200056) for 3 weeks, and finally returned to the GFD for recovery over 2, 6, 10, or 24 weeks. Age-matched naïve controls (non-sensitized on GFD with no gluten exposure) were used to determine normal and baseline values and compare against experimental groups. Mice receiving fiber-supplemented diets were transitioned over the first week with a 50:50 mixture of no added fiber GFD and either 52.8 g/kg inulin (IN, TD.2100884) diet or 136 g/kg HylonVII (RS, TD.210885) to allow the mice to acclimatize. The total fiber content in the supplemented diets was increased to approximately 15% from a grain-based chow formula with ~7.5% dietary fiber. Diet composition is listed in Table 2 and was calculated based on allometric species nutritional requirements and not direct mass-to-mass conversions64. Mice were monitored for signs of distress, changes in food consumption, weight gain, and fecal output through the duration of the diet intervention study.

Evaluation of gluten-immunopathology
Cross sections from the proximal small intestine were fixed in 10% formalin and embedded in paraffin for blinded evaluation using brightfield microscopy (Olympus) using open-source QuPath software65. The CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) were quantified by immunohistochemical staining23,66. The primary antibody, polyclonal rabbit anti human CD3 (A045229-2; Agilent), was diluted 1:1000 (1 μL in 1 mL of 1% BSA in PBS) and incubated overnight. CD3+ IELs were visualized with 3,3’-diamonobenzideine (DAB+ substrate chromogen system, K346811-2; Agilent) and counterstained with Mayer’s hematoxylin (S330930-2; Agilent) for 60 s. CD3+ IELs were quantified in 5 randomly chosen villi tips and reported as the number of IELs per 100 enterocytes. The same paraffin-embedded sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin for villus-height and crypt-depth measurements for the villus-to-crypt ratio (V/C). Ten villi and adjacent crypt pairs were randomly selected and measured. An equally weighted composite VCIEL scoring system was used to combine histological measures and create a standardized baseline around the naïve control group24. At necropsy, the small intestine was washed out and contents collected in 0.05 M EDTA in PBS with soy trypsin inhibitor (0.1 mg/mL; T9128-1G; Sigma) and phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride (0.8 mM; P7626; Sigma-Aldrich) to prevent protein degradation. Direct ELISA was performed to quantify anti-TG2 or anti-gliadin IgA antibodies in mouse luminal contents23,66. 96-well plates were coated with either transglutaminase in PBS (0.1 μg per well; T5398-2UN; Sigma-Aldrich) or gliadin dissolved in 70% ethanol and diluted in PBS (5 μg per well; G3375; Sigma-Aldrich). Non-specific binding was blocked with 2% BSA in PBS-Tween before a 2-h incubation of 50 μL small intestinal wash solution in triplicate. Detection with 1 h incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary anti-mouse IgA antibody (diluted 1:5000; 1040-05; Southern Biotech) followed by TMB substrate (Agilent) reaction for 20 min before measuring absorbance at 450 nm using a Spectramax M3 plate reader (Molecular Devices). OD values were normalized to the total amount of protein in the sample using a protein quantification assay (Bio-Rad) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Prevotellaceae cocktail colonization. Ten isolated strains from the Prevotellaceae family were obtained from the collection of Dr. Michael Surette’s Lab (McMaster University49,50), based on their reduced abundance in CeD (Table 4). Isolates’ identities were confirmed with MALDI-TOF and cultured anaerobically in BHI-3 for 48 h with agitation. NOD/DQ8 mice were gavaged with PBS (negative control) or approximately 1 million cells of each strain combined, given on days 1 and 3 of the inulin diet.

Metabolite determinations with gas chromatography mass spectrometry. A targeted selected ion monitoring (SIM) gas chromatography mass-spectrometry (GC-MS) protocol was used to quantify SCFA in the small intestinal washes and feces collected at endpoint. Samples were extracted with 10% isobutanol before the addition of 125 µL of 20 mM NaOH and 400 µL of chloroform. After mixing, 400 µL of the upper aqueous phase was transferred to a new tube before the addition of 80 µL isobutanol, 100 µL pyridine, and 70 µL H2O. Finally, 50 µL of isobutylchloroformate and 150 µL of hexane were added, mixed, and the upper aqueous phase was transferred to pre-slit autosampler vials. GC-MS measurements were carried out on an Agilent 5975C inert mass selective detector (MSD) equipped with an Agilent 7890A GC and an Agilent 7693 autosampler (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA, USA), in the Centre for Microbial Chemical Biology (CMCB) at McMaster University. Separation of the analytes was achieved on an Agilent (Santa Clara, CA, USA) DB-1MS UI (30 m x 0.25 mm x 0.25 µm) column. The injector, ion source, quadrupole and the GC-MS interface temperatures were 260, 230, 150, and 280 °C, respectively. The flow rate of helium carrier gas was kept at 1 mL/min. 1 µL of derivatized sample was injected in duplicate with a 4.5 min solvent delay time and split ratio of 10:1. The initial column temperature was 40 °C and held for 5 min, ramped to 165 °C at the rate of 10 °C/min, and then increased to 310 °C at the rate of 100 °C/min and kept at this temperature for 3 min. The total run time was 22 min. The ionization was carried out in the electron impact (EI) mode at 70 eV. The MS data were acquired in the SIM mode using GC-MS MassHunter and MS quantitative analysis. The identification of compounds was confirmed by the injection of pure standards and comparison of the retention time and target ions.

RNA extraction and quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (RT-qPCR). Mouse tissue samples from the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and proximal colon were collected in RNALater (Invitrogen) before RNA extraction using the RNEasy Mini kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Extracted RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using iScript Reverse Transcriptase (Bio-Rad) with SsoFast EvaGreen Supermix (Bio-Rad) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The qPCR cycling consisted of initial denaturation at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95 °C for 10 s and annealing/extension at 65 °C for 30 s. GAPDH was used as an endogenous control for normalization of gene expression, and data were reported as the fold change in expression in response to inulin compared to GFD alone. Validated primer sequences for mouse GPR41 (142345193c1) and GPR43 (22122727a1) were obtained from Primer Bank50. Bacterial RNA was extracted from human duodenal aspirate samples using a Stool Total RNA purification kit (Norgen Biotek) and cDNA was synthesized using SuperScriptTM IV Reverse Transcriptase (Invitrogen) with random hexamer primers (Thermo Scientific) according to manufacturer instructions. RNA quality was measured using the differential ratio amplicons (RAMP) method of the bacterial glutamine synthetase A transcript (glnA)67 as previously reported for feces61,68. Samples with negative RAMP were removed from analysis. Primers for α-amylase (K07405) and fructan β-fructosidase (K03332) were designed using Primer3 using the following sequences for K07405 (5’−3’: AGGGAATGTTGACAGAGGGC and AAGCGGAAGTTGTCACTTGC) and K03332 (5’−3’ CAGCGTATCTCTGGGCAGAA and AGATGATGGCCCCTTCTCCA). The qRT-PCR cycling consisted of initial denaturation at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 45 cycles of denaturation at 95 °C for 10 s, annealing at 62 °C for 30 s, and extension at 72 °C for 30 s, and normalized to the expression of glnA. Relative quantitation was performed using standard curves from serial dilutions of the PCR product of P. melaninogenica K07405 and K0333269.

Microbiota sequencing and predicted microbial function
After genomic DNA extraction, an established protocol consisting of a 2-stage nested polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify the variable regions 3–4 of the 16S rRNA gene from low biomass samples was used to sequence the mouse duodenum and human aspirates using the MiSeq Illumina platform9. Sequences were then processed in R, version 4.4.2, using the package Divisive Amplicon Denoising Algorithm 2 (DADA270) and the SILVA reference database, version 138.171. FastTree 272 was used to calculate a phylogenetic tree of sequences, and data were explored using the phyloseq package73. Functional predictions based on 16S rRNA sequences were made using PICRUSt218, annotated using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes database74. Beta-Diversity was calculated using the Aitchison distance75, and differences between groups were calculated using PERMANOVA. Taxonomic and functional microbial differences were evaluated using a generalized linear mixed model with a negative binomial distribution76 with adjustment for age and sex as confounding variables for patient data. Statistical differences between groups were identified using estimated marginal means using the emmeans package77. 16S rRNA gene sequences were deposited in Sequence Read Archive (PRJNA1256891).

FoodSeq (Sequencing, bioinformatic pipeline, and diversity analysis)
We performed DNA extraction on randomized fecal samples using the DNeasy PowerSoil Pro kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. We prepared libraries using a two-step PCR process78 using trnL g and h primers79–81. Primary PCR amplification was conducted as previously described81. Secondary PCR amplification contained 5 µL each of 2.5 µM forward and reverse indexing primers, 25 µL of 2X KAPA HiFi HotStart Ready Mix, 0.5 µL of 100X SYBR Green I, 9.5 µL nuclease-free water, and 5 µL of primary PCR product diluted 1:100 in nuclease-free water. Amplicon libraries were then cleaned and pooled as previously described81. Paired-end sequencing was carried out on an Illumina MiniSeq using a 300-cycle Mid kit (Illumina). We demultiplexed, trimmed, filtered, and denoised sequence reads using a QIIME282 pipeline v. 2023.5.1 with DADA270 plugin. Sequence reads were aligned to a custom trnL reference database81 (available at https://github.com/LAD-LAB/mbpipeline/blob/main/reference/trnLGH.fasta), and taxonomic assignments were made using assignSpecies() in the DADA2 R package v. 1.30.0. We calculated observed richness and Shannon diversity using estimate_richness() in the phyloseq73 R package v. 1.46.0 for each sample after removing taxa unassigned to any dietary species in our reference database. Principal component analysis was performed using prcomp(), centered and not scaled, on CLR-transformed relative abundance data. A distance matrix was then generated using Euclidean distance calculations. Prior to PERMANOVA, homogeneity of dispersion was assessed using betadisper(). PERMANOVA was performed using adonis2() in the vegan R package v. 2.6.6.183 with 999 permutations, adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity/race, with post hoc pairwise comparisons using pairwiseAdonis() v. 0.4.184, adjusting p-values using the Bonferroni method. Age was significant in the PERMANOVA model (df = 1, F=1.41, R2=0.028, p=0.039) but showed significant dispersion (p<0.05), indicating heterogeneous variance in dietary composition across ages, and was therefore interpreted with caution due to the assumption violation. The trnL gene sequences were deposited in the Sequence Read Archive (PRJNA1256896)

Statistical analysis
Data are presented for each individual sample (human or mouse). Graphpad Prism Version 10.4.2 was used for most statistical analyses and graph creation. R version 4.4.2 was used for the analysis of gene sequences. In Prism, all data were first tested for statistical outliers for exclusion (ROUT, Q=1%). For analysis in R, outliers were excluded if they exceeded 3 times the interquartile range. Data normality was then checked using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, such that non-parametric tests were used for non-normally distributed data. For comparisons between two groups, the Student’s t test or the nonparametric Mann–Whitney was used. For three or more groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used with Tukey’s post hoc test, or the nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis followed by Dunn’s test. A minimum threshold of p<0.05 was used to determine statistically significant effects.

Summary & General Comments
In the present study, Wulczynski et al. set up to investigate a critical gap in knowledge of celiac disease, namely targeting
the chronic fiber insufficiencies commonly observed in patients. They studied the microbial fiber metabolism in the small
intestine in adult patients with active and treated celiac disease and compared the results with healthy age-matched
controls. This manuscript presents an investigation into the relationship between dietary fiber intake, gut microbiota
composition, and gastrointestinal symptoms, complemented by an animal model to explore potential mechanisms. They

microbial fiber metabolism in the small intestine which associates with depletion of the carbolytic taxa Prevotella spp. To
further investigate this mechanistically, they next sensitized mice with transgenic expression HLA-DQ8 gene in non-obese
diabetic background (NOD/DQ8) with gluten to determine timing of mucosal recovery after 2, 6, 10, and 24 weeks of gluten-
free diet. After 10 weeks of gluten-free diet (GFD) when sensitized NOD/DQ8 mice normalized histological parameters, the
effect of fiber supplementation with either inulin or HylonVII supplemented for 6 weeks.
They found that supplementation with inulin during GFD improved histology versus the no added fiber group, whereas
HylonVII did not normalize IELs, but had improved histology versus the no added fiber group. All mice became seronegative
after 12 weeks of inulin or HylonVII. More importantly, colonization with Prevotella spp increased small intestinal short chain
fatty acids (SCFA) with inulin supplementation during GFD, compared with no added fiber. Based on these results, the
authors conclude that the small intestinal microbiota in adult patients with active or treated celiac disease patients contains
less fiber-degrading bacteria and that certain fibers could be used as adjuvant therapy for the gluten-free diet to promote
mucosal healing.
Fiber insufficiency and microbiome dysbiosis are topics of importance in celiac disease, especially if studied prospectively,
although this study centers around individuals already with the disease. However, while the introduction raises important
points, the study design and evidence presented do not adequately address the key gaps and limitations initially outlined.
While a mechanistic model is used, there are challenges in translatability to a clinical context in humans. The central
message is a bit unclear and hard to follow and can be improved to strengthen the paper.
Here are some specific comments for the authors to consider when revising their manuscript.
Major Concerns
• The exclusive use of 16S rRNA sequencing and PICRUSt is a critical limitation, especially given the small sample size of
both the human and mouse arms of this paper. PICRUSt inherently does not allow robust functional inference. At minimum,
shotgun metagenomics should have been used, if not also metatranscriptomics, especially given the small sample size in
both the human and mouse arms of this study. This would greatly strengthen the paper. Drawing strong functional
conclusions based on imputed gene content, given the tone and scope of this paper (centered around microbial metabolic
potential as it relates to fiber), is not sufficient.
• It is notable that some of the reported findings are only marginally significant (e.g., Prevotella, p=0.07). We appreciate that
these samples are challenging to obtain, but with a low n and high inter-individual variability in adults, the authors should be
cautious of overinterpretation. Again, metagenomics would help overcome these limitations and make the findings more
robust. The rationale for selecting 10 Prevotellaceae strains is unclear, especially given that not all were significantly
associated with human data.
• The authors report no correlation between fiber intake and gastrointestinal scores in patients with celiac disease (page 6),
yet they proceed as though fiber depletion plays a key role in symptoms. This contradiction is not acknowledged or
reconciled in the discussion.
• Regarding the attempt to address potential mechanisms, there are some challenges in the present design. There is no
well-validated mouse model for celiac disease. This should be noted as a limitation. The use of histology in germ-free mice
is not a sufficient substitute and should be discussed more critically.
• The diet intervention in the mice is undermined by the extreme dosages, which simply cannot scale to human study. The
doses of inulin (52.8 g/kg) and Hylon VII (136 g/kg) used in mice are extraordinarily high and would be impractical and
unsafe in humans, likely resulting in significant GI distress. The manuscript should estimate human-equivalent doses and
discuss feasibility and tolerability (e.g., https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4804402/. Using the formula HED = animal
dose x[Km_mouse/Km_human] (or 3/37), the doses used by the authors equate to 299 g/day of inulin and 772 g/day of
resistant starch for a 70-kg human. These levels far exceed tolerable human intakes (typically 5–15 g/day for inulin and 20–
40 g/day for resistant starch), and would likely cause significant GI distress, making them unfeasible for human consumption
and especially problematic for celiac disease patients. To put this in context, 772 g of resistant starch is equivalent to ~1.7 lb
of purified starch or >22 lb of cooked green bananas/potatoes. Similarly, 299 g of inulin equals ~1.5 lb of raw chicory root.
This exercise underscores a fundamental issue in the design and by extension, translational relevance. While the diets may
be commercially available by Envigo (Inotiv), they are not translatable. No dosage response experiments were conducted.
The HED calculations call into question the feasibility, safety, interpretability, and real-world relevance of these experiments.
• Bridging the human data and the mouse model more explicitly might enhance the study’s overall flow. How do the authors
interpret the lack of microbial changes after inulin treatment in mice? Does this undercut one of the core premises? Are
microbial dysbiotic shifts seen after supplementation with Prevotella in addition to inulin?
Minor Suggestions
• The introduction would benefit from additional references studying celiac disease in adults, as microbiome stability and
resilience differ significantly by age group, i.e., the bacterial differences observed in very young children with (or preceding)
celiac disease may not be the same as those experienced by adults with new-onset or treated celiac disease.
• The effects of diet + bacterial supplementation on microbial dynamics are warranted, which was not presented.
• Supplementary Figure 2b is missing.
• The authors colonized mice with specific strains of bacteria from the human study. It is important to address in the paper
that Prevotella is not universally beneficial. For example, P. copri has been linked to both pro- and anti-inflammatory roles,
including associations with RA and JIA, other autoimmune diseases that are also often comorbid with celiac. The
manuscript does not discuss this nuance, nor the delivery challenges associated with strict anaerobes.
• The sample size could be problematic in this study. A power analysis within the methods or beginning of results or
addressing this further with a statement on generalizability is therefore warranted.
• Discuss whether any microbial changes were observed after combined supplementation with inulin and Prevotella—this is
alluded to but not clearly reported.
Other Remarks
• The figures are clear and very well done, for instance Figure 5. They are easy to follow. The panels demonstrating study
design (like Figure 3a) are especially helpful to the reader. Colors for Hylon VII and inulin are consistent across figures,
which facilitates understanding and flow of the results. The histological findings in this and other figures for gluten
immunopathology using brightfield microscopy are a strength of the paper.
Conclusion
Although the study presents interesting findings with therapeutic potential and potential novel insights in the etiopathology of
celiac disease, it also has some methodological limitations and ambiguous results. Although it is noteworthy that soluble
fiber inulin accelerated mucosal healing by supporting carbolytic activity of the small intestinal microbiota in the mouse, a
limitation lies in studying patients either at diagnosis with active celiac disease or in clinical remission after prolonged
gluten-free diet, as both states complicate interpretation of causality in microbial alterations. It remains unresolved whether
impaired microbial fiber metabolism is a contributing factor to disease pathogenesis or a consequence of mucosal injury,
raising the fundamental question of causality.

We would like to thank the editors and reviewers for their thorough and thoughtful comments.

Point-by-point answer to Reviewers’ comments:

given the small sample size of both the human and mouse arms of this paper. PICRUSt
inherently does not allow robust functional inference. At minimum, shotgun metagenomics

We agree that PICRUSt2 is mainly focused on prediction of bacterial core genomes and has
lower resolution for functional inference compared with shotgun metagenomics. However, 16S
rRNA gene sequencing and functional predictions are still relevant (Jovel et al., 2016), especially
for low biomass samples. On the other hand, metagenomics or metatranscriptomics analysis of
the duodenum predominantly captures host-derived DNA and transcripts. Duodenal aspirates
have low bacterial biomass and a high host-to-microbe DNA ratio, making metagenomic
approaches difficult, less reliable, and more costly (Caminero et al., 2025; Jervis-Bardy et al.,
2015; Matchado et al., 2024). Removing the host DNA from low biomass samples remains a
challenge for small intestinal microbiota research. New techniques are being proposed but, we
will need to wait to have those validated specifically for proximal small intestinal biopsies from
the duodenum and jejunum, as well as luminal aspirates. Thus, we employed 16S rRNA gene
sequencing, as our study targeted a low-biomass site and utilized a method that was previously
validated for this condition in humans (Constante et al., 2022). We however acknowledge these
limitations and raise the methodology constraints of shotgun metagenomics and
metatranscriptomics in low yield ecosystems in the discussion (Pg 14, lines- 297-300). We agree
that while PICRUSt is most valuable as a data mining tool (Jovel et al., 2016), ideally predictions
should be confirmed using other methods. Our group has previously used PICRUSt to guide the
analysis of bacterial stool transcripts to confirm how the presence of the gene and the mRNA
expression (similar to what one may obtain in a metatranscriptomics analysis) affect microbial
function and result in disease activity (Cholet et al., 2019; Santiago et al., 2023). Thus, to address
the reviewers’ point we completed a similar experiment to validate the expression of glycoside
hydrolases in the aspirates using targeted quantitative reverse-transcriptase PCR. The
quantification of bacterial RNA demonstrates not only the relevance of the PICRUSt predictions
but also, as suggested by the reviewer, it goes one step further by quantifying RNA expression
instead of DNA levels. We thank the reviewer for this comment as we believe it made the results
stronger by including this transcript-level data. This result is included in Supplementary Figure
2c, and we also briefly discuss it in limitations paragraph (Discussion, page 14).
Page 5 (line 102 – 106):
“To confirm the PICRUSt2-predicted results, we performed qRT-PCRs for the highest abundance
bacterium identified at the species level (Prevotella 7 melaninogenica) for genes K07405 and
K03332. We found that K07405 had a similar RNA expression profile as the predicted gene content
with reduced expression in CeD compared with controls. No statistical differences were observed
for K03332 (Supplementary Figure 2c)”.
Supplementary figure 2c:

provide more robust functional analysis than 16S rRNA gene sequencing, especially if they include
jejunum or ileum, but could not be completed in our low-biomass duodenal aspirates due to high

were significantly associated with human data.”
Response:
We have now revised the discussion to expand on the rationale for the selection of

bacteria (Lau et al., 2016; Whelan et al., 2020). We centered on species belonging to
Prevotellaceae, which is a family of bacteria that are at high abundance in the oral cavity and
colonize the small intestine (Könönen & Gursoy, 2022; Tett et al., 2021). They are known to be a
fiber-degrading taxa with capacity for SCFA production (Chen et al., 2017; Prasoodanan P. K. et
al., 2021) due to the many glycoside hydrolase enzymes they carry in addition to the two
identified in our study (α-amylase and fructan- β-fructosidase). Our observation that the relative
abundance of Prevotella spp is decreased in CeD compared with healthy controls is supported by
our previous paper (Constante et al. 2022), and other independent cohorts (Nistal et al., 2012;
Roque et al., 2024). Thus, given that our mouse SPF colony contained a low relative abundance
of Prevotellaceae, we designed a mechanistic experiment in gnotobiotic mice using well
characterized Prevotellaceae strains from Surette’s lab collection at McMaster to functionally
validate their role in fiber metabolism and SCFA production in the small intestine. This is now
better explained in the discussion of the revised manuscript on page 12.
Page 12 (lines 266-273)
“The relative abundance of Prevotella spp was low in the mouse small intestine and was not
significantly affected by either fiber diet. Thus, we designed a mechanistic experiment by
colonizing germ-free mice with a collection of Prevotella spp from our biobank of human derived
bacteria (Lau et al., 2016; Whelan et al., 2020). These species were all confirmed to carry the
genes of interest for α-amylase (K07405) and fructan-β-fructosidase (K03332), and in colonized

Response:
Thank you for this important comment and the opportunity to clarify it. Our study was not
designed to investigate symptoms in celiac disease in response to fiber challenge or
supplementation or due to differences in fiber intake. This would require a different design, such
as a clinical study with dietary interventions, and longitudinal tracking of symptom responses
and dietary evaluations. The results of our study could help better design such an intervention or
longitudinal study by providing valuable mechanistic insight and microbial (structure and
function) targets. In our cohort, the estimated fiber intake did not correlate with gastrointestinal
symptoms rating scores patients were reporting at a cross-sectional level. There was no fiber
challenge; patients were on their usual diet and only T-CeD were on a GFD. Many participants
were below the recommended fiber intake levels, and this was more evident in the GFD group.
We do not claim that fiber plays a role in symptoms in this study, although there is literature that
suggests some IBD patients can be intolerant to some fibers (Armstrong et al., 2023), and these
studies are cited as general background to highlight beneficial and detrimental effects of fiber as
shown by others. We were intrigued though by the finding that dietary fiber intake did not fully
explain the lower saccharolytic activity observed in CeD patients. This suggested a primary
microbial functional deficiency, rather than lack of dietary substrate, motivating the mechanistic
studies. We have explained this better in the manuscript on page 10.
Page 10 (lines 203-208)
“There was no relationship between estimated fiber consumption and symptoms in our cohort,
although many participants were already consuming lower than recommended fiber. Our study
was not designed to investigate fiber intolerance in humans with CeD, as has been done previously
in inflammatory bowel disease (Armstrong et al., 2023; Kuang & Binion, 2022), but to investigate
the impact of diet on microbial saccharolytic function in the small intestine.”
“Regarding the attempt to address potential mechanisms, there are some challenges in the
present design. There is no well-validated mouse model for celiac disease. This should be
noted as a limitation. The use of histology in germ-free mice is not a sufficient substitute
and should be discussed more critically.”
Response:
No animal model will ever reproduce human disease completely and there is no human disease
for which there is a single animal model. For instance, in IBD, T cell transfer, DSS, TNBS, IL-
is no reason why there should be only one model for CeD, rather a large toolbox of in vitro and
in vivo models should complement clinical interventions and samples, including organoids.
We would like to share a quote from a commentary from the Scientific Advisory Board for AGA
Center for Gut Microbiome Research and Education that specifically addresses the role of animal
models in GI disease:
“Preclinical models of disease … aim to reproduce specific features of the disease being
studied, leading to new insights that require validation in humans. The three key
aspects traditionally used to evaluate preclinical models relate to (1, face validity) the
features of the disease being modelled, (2, construct validity) whether the features of the
model arise for biologically relevant reasons, and (3, predictive validity) how well the
model predicts expression of those pathways or responses to treatment in humans...”
(Britton et al., 2024).
We agree that there is no perfect model for any human disease (including celiac disease) and,
that models are used based on the 3 criteria above and depending on the question under study.
For celiac disease, most current animal models are based on MHC class II transgenic mice
expressing HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8, which can, or not, include transgenic expression of IL-15 to
study particularly that pathway, but no single mouse model recapitulates all features of human
disease. With respect to the NOD-DQ8 model, it expresses the human DQ8 gene in the absence
of endogenous mouse MHC-II and it has extensively been characterized for the study of gluten-
specific immune responses at the Mayo Clinic (Black et al., 2002; Marietta et al., 2004; Verdu et
al., 2008). The model was further validated by our group and others for the past 15-20 years to
study the influence of microbial colonization and composition on gluten-induced
immunopathology (Bodkhe et al., 2021; Caminero et al., 2016, 2019; Galipeau et al., 2015;
Lamas et al., 2020), demonstrating face and to certain extent, construct validity. More recently,
the group of Detlef Schuppan (U of Mainz) has used this model to study mechanistic pathways,
and reproduce effectiveness of the TG2 inhibitor ZED1227, showing promising predictive
validity (unpublished, presented at UEGW 2025). Thus, in our opinion the model is useful to
complement our clinical observations and to study microbial pathogenesis as the model shows
microbial colonization affects and modulates gluten immunopathology.
We believe the strength of our paper is the use of a variety of experimental tools including
gnotobiotic mouse models for direct interrogation of specific microbial function
(Prevotellaceae), functional assays, molecular biology and biochemistry and validations in
clinical cohorts, truly encompassing what translational research should represent. This is now
discussed in limitations on Page 14.
Page 14 (lines 302-308)
“ … the NOD/DQ8 mouse employed here requires sensitization and the use of a microbial
adjuvant and is well suited for the study of environmental triggers or modulators of disease
severity (Caminero, McCarville, Galipeau, et al., 2019) and fulfills validity criteria of animal
models (Britton et al., 2024) such as ability to produce mechanistic insight, for clinical trial
validation. This translational study provides unique insight into the relevance of fiber
supplementation in improving gluten-specific immunity through microbial metabolism, a finding
that warrants further evaluation in clinical trials using human-equivalent doses.”
“The diet intervention in the mice is undermined by the extreme dosages, which simply
cannot scale to human study. The doses of inulin (52.8 g/kg) and Hylon VII (136 g/kg) used
in mice are extraordinarily high and would be impractical and unsafe in humans, likely
resulting in significant GI distress. The manuscript should estimate human-equivalent
doses and discuss feasibility and tolerability
(e.g., https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4804402/). This exercise underscores a
fundamental issue in the design and by extension, translational relevance. While the diets
may be commercially available by Envigo (Inotiv), they are not translatable. No dosage
response experiments were conducted. The HED calculations call into question the
feasibility, safety, interpretability, and real-world relevance of these experiments.”
Response:
Our study was not intended to determine human doses of fiber supplementation in future studies.
The value of our study is the mechanistic demonstration that some fibers can influence the
function of the small intestinal microbiome differentially. This concept will be important to
better design future challenge studies in humans, for instance for the choice of biogeographic
location of fiber-microbiome interactions and taxa of interest as outcomes. Our study did not
evaluate effective doses in humans, which we clarify now in the revised Discussion.
We would like to further explain how our calculations for the mouse feed were done. As
reviewers suggest, doses based on mass, are well suited for calculations of “human equivalent
doses” of pharmacological intervention or drugs. However, these conversions are less
appropriate for studies like ours incorporating nutritional substrates in mouse feeds. The
formulation of the animal diets used in our study is based on allometric scaling which was
calculated to consider how the metabolic and biological processes scale with the size of the
animal (Rucker, 2022). When using direct mass conversion, the assumption is that the human
would require 2500-2800 times more nutrients than the mouse. However, when using metabolic
calculations based on resting energy expenditure, humans only require 200-400 times more
energy than mice. Therefore, we calculate that the equivalent dose for humans could range from
40-80g inulin daily, which is slightly higher than the currently recommended doses by Health
Canada for females (25g/d) and males (38g/d). The transition to the fiber-supplemented diets
though was performed progressively not all at once; allowing the mice in our study to acclimate
to a reduced dose of fiber over the first week, ensuring they were well adapted to the higher
doses. Moreover, as the fiber was incorporated in the feed (not by a challenge), ingestion was
physiological.
An unknown factor to consider is the relative contribution of the microbiota to metabolism;
and how disease-associated alterations in microbiota can further impact metabolism in vivo
(Caminero et al., 2016; Caminero, McCarville, Zevallos, et al., 2019). This is now explained in
methods:

Finally, during our study, the mice were monitored for potential signs of distress, food

Response:
Thank you for this comment. We now better explain these findings. Changes in the relative
abundance of different taxa (see new supplementary Fig 6b, included below as well for the
reviewer) were observed following inulin supplementation, however, overall clustering
according to β-diversity was not affected when inulin and Hylon VII-fed mice were compared.
We do not see this as “undercutting any premise”, as composition and diversity reflect different
aspects of ecology. For example, diversity metrics summarize overall richness and evenness, so
specific taxa can change without affecting total diversity. This occurs when shifts in some
microbes are balanced by opposing changes in others. Due to the inherent inter-variability of the
microbiome, we agree that it is more appropriate to describe the observed changes or shifts after
an intervention.
Supplementary figure 6b displays the microbial taxa that were significantly affected by the diet
intervention at endpoint. Changes in the relative abundance of several taxa were observed
between the different groups, suggesting distinct effects of fiber interventions on the small
intestinal microbiome. In the revised version we summarize these changes in the text as follows:

groups (Fig. 4b). Specifically, HylonVII had higher Helicobacter, Alistepes, Aneroplamasma,

and lower abundance of Roseburia, Turicibacter, Parasutterella, Desulfovibrio, Dorea,

higher Faecalibaculum, Gemella, Staphylococcus, Coriobacteriaceae UCG.002 and lower

“Are microbial dysbiotic shifts seen after supplementation with Prevotella in addition to
inulin?”
Response:
We prefer not to refer to “dysbiosis”, as this is a term that is not easy to define, in the same way,
it is difficult to define “eubiosis” (Britton et al., 2024). Instead, we describe the significant shifts
after interventions. In experiments using SPF mice, the relative abundance of Prevotella in the
mouse duodenum was less than 1% and did not significantly expand when fed inulin compared
with the no added fiber GFD. We have clarified this in the discussion on page 12.
Prevotellaceae were used exclusively to colonize germ-free mice that were kept gnotobiotically
to test a specific role of this taxon in the functional response to fiber (the rationale for using
Prevotellaceae is explained above in an earlier response). Prevotella histicola has been
previously demonstrated as beneficial in the NOD-DQ8 model (Bodkhe et al., 2021).
Supplementation of SPF mice with 108 CFU Prevotella spp, would not be expected to cause
“overgrowth”, as this is usually the probiotic dose administered to mice (for humans daily doses
can reach up to 5x1010) which can range between 10x8 to 10x11 CFUs (Bodkhe et al., 2021;
Caminero, McCarville, Zevallos, et al., 2019; McCarville et al., 2017; Natividad et al., 2012).
Moreover, the newly administered taxon would never colonize permanently an SPF mouse and
would disappear within 48 hours after stopping administration. This has well been demonstrated
in murine and human probiotic supplementation studies (Laursen et al., 2017; Zmora et al.,
2018). Furthermore, fiber consumption, Prevotella relative abundance, and SCFA are all
positively associated with decreased risk of developing food allergy (Goldberg et al., 2020;
Vuillermin et al., 2020), supporting the notion of members of this taxon have potential use in
microbial therapeutics, that will need to be confirmed in human studies (Itano et al., 2023).

bacteria (Lau et al., 2016; Whelan et al., 2020). These species were all confirmed to carry the
genes of interest for α-amylase (K07405) and fructan-β-fructosidase (K03332), and in colonized
mice, they increased small intestinal SCFA upon inulin supplementation.”

Response: Thank you for this comment. We show Faith’s PD figure to account for changes in
phylogenetic diversity which reflects changes in function due to evolutionary proximity, more
than changes in species richness or evenness alone. We agree with the reviewer that this limits
interpretation on evenness analysis or simple richness. We therefore added in the revised
manuscript Chao1 and Shannon diversity measures for the microbiota in Supplementary Fig 1,
which have similar results. We also complemented those with the microbial Beta-diversity and
relative abundance plots in Supplementary Fig 1 and 2.
Figure 2 Results: “Why was Shannon diversity used as the sole alpha-diversity metric in
this section? How does this choice relate to earlier use of Faith’s PD? The authors should
consider using multiple complementary metrics throughout the paper.”
Response: The analysis for FoodSeq plant DNA was completed independently from the
microbiota analysis. Shannon diversity was chosen because it accounts for both species richness
and evenness, without relying on phylogenetic relationships. This approach was intentionally
chosen as the trnL gene region that was amplified is shorter (length ranging from 50-150bp) than
the bacterial 16S V3V4 regions, providing less phylogenetic resolution between closely related
taxa. Furthermore, the evolutionary distances in plants do not necessarily translate to nutritional
differences relevant in the human diet. Please note that the primary goal of FoodSeq Plant DNA
is to estimate dietary plant intake through fecal DNA profiling, rather than to assess ecological
dynamics, which is what the metrics used in microbiome studies capture.

• Hylon VII—although 70% RS2—is only 12% fiber (at least according to the

ability to ask if dietary fiber can improve CeD outcomes. This choice of “fiber” also

results section and the corresponding discussion need to be re-written to reflect what
the authors are actually feeding to mice.

and inulin—for instance, the HylonVII dose is nearly 3X the inulin dose—why?
Calculating the human dose equivalent would also be helpful.”
Response:
Thank you for allowing us to clarify this. Our rodent diets are grain-based chow with additional
prebiotic supplements. This means that the mice get a variety of different natural fibers,
compared to a purified diet where the intervention is all or nothing. Our choice for including
HylonVII (Ingredion 03451B00) was based on its potential as prebiotic candidate to investigate
alongside the GFD. HylonVII and other type 2 resistant starches are considered prebiotic fibers
by North American and European governing agencies for their beneficial properties (EFSA Panel
on Dietetic Products and Allergies (NDA), 2010; Sobh et al., 2022). HylonVII contains 70%
amylose and is estimated to contain 48% bioavailable RS2 prebiotic substrate (Le Leu et al.,
2009). It is difficult to directly compare the amount of different prebiotic substrates for an
intervention in an animal model, so the diets were formulated to contain similar amounts of
bioavailable carbohydrates and caloric density, which is why there is such a large difference in
mass of ingredients (Table 2). The total fiber/prebiotic substrate from all sources in both diets
was formulated to be 15%. The vendor Envigo (Inotiv) supplied the inulin (TIC Prestested Inulin
LV-110 Powder (Ingredion 38910903) and HylonVII for the diets in consultation with us and
their specialized technicians. Specifically, we revised the Hylon VII diet with expert Envigo
technologists and the values for NDF for the natural ingredients are described in a sheet that can
be appended to the manuscript if the editors consider it necessary. Fiber content was calculated
using the formulas below:
o Inulin diet fiber: dietNDF + dietFiber - Inulin fiber calc + Inulin = 158.5 g/kg (15.8%)
o H7 diet fiber: dietNDF + dietFiber - H7 fiber calc + (0.48*H7) = 155 g/kg (15.5%)
Calculations for human equivalent doses based on mass are less appropriate for nutritional
studies like ours than pharmacological interventions. The formulation of the animal diets used in
our study is based on allometric scaling which was calculated to consider how the metabolic and
biological processes scale with the size of the animal (Rucker, 2022). Another factor to consider
is the relative contribution of the microbiota to metabolism; and how diseased-associated
alterations in microbiota can further impact metabolism in vivo (Caminero et al., 2016;
Caminero, McCarville, Zevallos, et al., 2019). This is now explained better in methods on page
18.

Figure 3 Results: “Current microbiome analyses appear to be limited only to endpoint
analyses, which is disappointing. More information about the microbiomes at baseline
before fiber interventions and prior to disease induction would provide a more thorough
analysis.”
Response:
Our design was limited to endpoint analysis because these tissue samples could only be collected
at necropsy and cannot be completed longitudinally (paired), unlike feces. The primary outcome
was to investigate in parallel (cross-sectional), with appropriate controls, the changes in the
small intestinal microbiome that accompanied improvements in immunopathology over time
with different prebiotic substrates compared to the no added fiber GFD. The longitudinal
sampling of the small intestine in mice would require sacrifice at different timepoints and would
be comparing different mice as there is not available technique to obtain mucosal biopsies in vivo
from the mouse duodenum. The NAF GFD group is well suited as a parallel control comparison
against the inulin or HylonVII fed mice in the context of recovery from gluten exposure on a
gluten-free diet. All the mice were housed in the same room of a well-controlled SPF facility that
is regularly monitored for the absence of exogenous contaminations pathogens. Moreover, at the
start of the study, and anticipating this, we distributed mice from same litters to all treatment
groups, minimizing biases at baseline due to cage effects. This is better explained under methods
in the revised manuscript on page 17:

“To minimize litter and cage effects, littermates were distributed across treatment groups using
random assignment to sex-balanced cages before sensitization with gluten using a previously
established protocol (Galipeau et al., 2011).”.
